tool.name: dupRadar
tool.description: assess PCR duplication in RNA-seq data as a function of expression
tool.command: #import re ## drop .bam so the MultiQC row can line up with the same sample's other QC rows #set $sample = re.sub(r'[^\w.-]', '_', re.sub(r'\.bam$', '', str($input.element_identifier))) ln -s '$input' input.bam && ln -s '$gtf' annotation.gtf && Rscript '$dupradar_script' '$sample' $stranded $paired_end '$advanced.feature_type' '$advanced.attr_type' $plot_format $multiqc

param.name: input
param.label: Duplicate-marked BAM file
param.help: Reads must be aligned and have PCR duplicates flagged but not removed, e.g. by Picard MarkDuplicates

param.name: stranded
param.label: Library strandedness
param.help: Same convention as featureCounts: forward means read 1 maps to the gene's strand

param.name: paired_end
param.label: Paired-end reads?
param.help: Paired-end data are counted as fragments

param.name: multiqc
param.label: Write MultiQC custom-content files?
param.help: The duplication intercept for the general statistics table and the fitted curve, in the format nf-core/rnaseq produces

validator.message: Letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores only

param.name: attr_type
param.label: GTF attribute that groups features into genes

validator.message: Letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores only

tool.help:
## What it does
dupRadar measures how the PCR duplication rate of an RNA-seq library depends on gene expression. Highly expressed genes are expected to carry many duplicate reads simply because their fragments are sampled so often. A high duplication rate among *lowly* expressed genes instead points to a library with low complexity or heavy PCR amplification.
The tool counts reads per gene four times with featureCounts: with and without the reads flagged as duplicates, each with and without multi-mapping reads. It reports the duplication rate per gene against reads per kilobase (RPK). It then fits a logistic regression of duplication rate on log10(RPK).
## Input
- A **coordinate-sorted BAM with duplicates marked**, not removed. dupRadar does not mark duplicates itself: run Picard MarkDuplicates (or an equivalent that sets the SAM `0x400` flag) first. On an unmarked BAM every duplication rate is 0. - The gene annotation in **GTF** format used for the alignment. - The library strandedness and whether the reads are paired. Paired-end is the default here; switch it off for single-end data, which featureCounts refuses to count as paired.
Under *Annotation options*, the GTF feature type (default `exon`) and the attribute that groups features into genes (default `gene_id`) are passed to featureCounts as `GTF.featureType` and `GTF.attrType`.
## Output
- **Duplication matrix**: one row per gene with read counts with and without duplicates (unique and multi-mapping), RPK, and the duplication rate. - **Intercept and slope** of the fitted logistic model, reported (as dupRadar does) on the odds scale. The intercept is the odds of a read being a duplicate for a gene at 1 read/kbp, so it stays near 0 for a clean library; the slope is the factor by which those odds grow with each 10-fold increase in expression. The labels in this file match what nf-core/rnaseq writes. - **Density scatter plot** of duplication rate against RPK with the fitted curve, the most useful single view of the library. - **Boxplot** of duplication rate by expression bin and a **histogram** of RPK values. - Optionally, two **MultiQC custom-content** tables in the style nf-core/rnaseq writes: the intercept for the general statistics table, and points sampled from the fitted curve. They carry MultiQC's in-file headers, but Galaxy's MultiQC tool sets its own custom-content options, so choose *generalstats* and *linegraph* there to match.
## Interpreting the plot
In a good library the duplication rate stays low for genes below about 1 read/bp (1,000 reads/kbp on the plot's x axis, marked by the red dashed line) and rises only above it, where reads start to pile up on the same positions by chance. A curve that starts high on the left (a high intercept) indicates technical duplication. See the [dupRadar vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/dupRadar/inst/doc/dupRadar.html) for examples.
